The term used to describe some types of treatment of prostate cancer. Involves the removal of a body part or the destruction of its function through the use of surgery, hormones, drugs, heat, chemicals, electrocautery, or other methods.

Abbreviated ARF; sudden onset of kidney failure characterized by uremia. May be caused by the kidneys not receiving enough blood to filter due to dehydration or a sudden drop in blood volume or blood pressure from injury, burns, or a severe infection. Can be fatal if not reversed promptly.
The absence of urine formation by the kidneys. Often caused by kidney failure or a urinary tract obstruction.

Abbreviated BPH; also known as benign prostatic hypertrophy or an enlarged prostate. An enlargement of the prostate gland that most often occurs in men older than age 50. Can make urination difficult and causes other urinary tract problems for men. Hyperplasia is an increase in cell numbers typically associated with tumor growth; in this case, it is not caused by cancer or infection.
Abbreviated CKD; the progressive loss of renal function over months or years. May result from diabetes mellitus, hypertension, or a family history of kidney disease. Can be life-threatening.
An inflammation of the bladder.
Also known as a prolapsed bladder; a hernia of the bladder through the vaginal wall. Sometimes occurs as a result of pregnancy or childbirth.
A stone located within the urinary bladder.
The visual examination of the urinary bladder with the use of a specialized type of endoscope known as a cystoscope.

A procedure to remove waste products, such as urea, creatinine, and excess water from the blood of a patient whose kidneys no longer function. The two types in common use are hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis.
The increased output of urine.
Difficult or painful urination. Frequently associated with urinary tract infections.

A congenital condition in which one kidney is located in an abnormal position or has fused with the other kidney. Ectopic means located in an abnormal place or position. Can be associated with an increased risk of urinary tract infections and nephroliths.
breakdown_text: ec-: out ; top: place ; -ic: pertaining to

definition: Swelling caused by excessive fluid accumulation in body tissues that can be symptomatic of nephrotic syndrome and other kidney diseases. The swelling can be in the area around the eyes, or in the legs and feet.

Abbreviated ESRD; also known as kidney failure. The final stage of chronic kidney disease; fatal unless the functions of the failed kidneys are replaced by dialysis, or with a successful kidney transplant.
A congenital abnormality of the urethral opening. In the male, the opening is located on the upper surface of the penis; in the female, the urethral opening is in the region of the clitoris.

Abbreviated ESWL; the most common kidney stone treatment. High-energy ultrasonic waves traveling through water or gel are used to break the stone into fragments, which are then excreted in the urine. Extracorporeal means situated or occurring outside the body.
A type of nephritis caused by inflammation of the glomeruli that causes red blood cells and proteins to leak into the urine.

The process by which waste products are filtered directly from the patient's blood. Performed on an external hemodialysis machine, sometimes referred to as an artificial kidney. The most common type of dialysis.
breakdown_text: hem/o: blood ; dia: complete or through ; -lysis: separation

definition: The dilation (swelling) of one or both kidneys. Can be caused by problems associated with the backing up of urine due to an obstruction such as a nephrolith (kidney stone) or a stricture (narrowing) in the ureter.
breakdown_text: hydr/o: water ; nephr: kidney ; -osis: abnormal condition or disease

definition: The distention (swelling) of the ureter with urine that cannot flow because of a ureteral obstruction. Always accompanies hydronephrosis.
The presence of abnormally high concentrations of protein in the urine.
The presence of abnormally low concentrations of protein in the blood. Often associated with hyperproteinuria.
breakdown_text: hypo-: deficient or decreased ; protein: protein ; -emia: blood condition

definition: A congenital abnormality of the urethral opening. In the male, the urethral opening is on the ventral surface (underside) of the penis; in the female, the urethra opens into the vagina.
The inability to control the excretion of urine, feces, or both.

A chronic inflammation within the walls of the bladder. The symptoms are similar to those of cystitis; however, they do not respond to traditional treatment. Interstitial means relating to spaces within a tissue or organ.

Abbreviated IVP; a set of x-ray images of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder using an intravenous contrast medium to clearly visualize the structures. The process of creating the images is called intravenous pyelography. Used to diagnose changes in the urinary tract resulting from nephroliths, infections, enlarged prostate, tumors, and internal injuries after an abdominal trauma.
breakdown_text: pyel/o: renal pelvis ; -gram: a picture or record

definition: Also known as a kidney stone or renal calculus; a stone found in the kidney.
The presence of stones in the kidney.
The surgical freeing of a kidney from adhesions. The suffix -lysis also means destruction, so the term can also describe a pathologic condition in which there is destruction of renal cells.
The microscopic functional units of each kidney, where urine is produced through the processes of filtration, reabsorption, and secretion. Each nephron contains a glomerulus and a renal tubule.
Any disease of the kidney. Includes both degenerative and inflammatory conditions.

The placement of a catheter to maintain an opening from the pelvis of one or both kidneys to the exterior of the body. In a kidney affected by hydronephrosis, this allows urine to be drained directly through the lower back. Nephrostomy tubes are also used to gain access to the kidneys for diagnostic procedures.

Also known as nephrosis; a group of conditions in which excessive amounts of protein are lost through the urine. Usually caused by damage to the glomeruli, resulting in abnormally low levels of protein in the blood.
A urinary problem caused by interference with the normal nerve pathways associated with urination.
Frequent and excessive urination during the night.
Urinary incontinence during sleep; also known as bed-wetting. Nocturnal means pertaining to night.
Scanty urination. Can be caused by dehydration, renal failure, or a urinary tract obstruction. Oliguria is the opposite of polyuria.

Abbreviated PCNL; the surgical removal of a nephrolith through a small incision in the back. A small tube is temporarily inserted through the incision into the kidney; the stone is crushed and the pieces are removed. Used if ESWL has not been successful, if an infection is present, or if the stone is particularly large. Percutaneous means performed through the skin.
breakdown_text: nephr/o: kidney ; lith: stone ; -otomy: surgical incision

definition: Dialysis in which the lining of the peritoneal cavity acts as a filter to remove waste from the blood. Sterile dialysate flows into the peritoneal cavity through a catheter implanted in the abdominal wall, is left in to absorb waste products, and is then drained out. Can be done at home but is considered less effective than hemodialysis.

Abbreviated PKD; a genetic disorder characterized by the growth of numerous fluid-filled cysts in the kidneys. These cysts slowly replace much of the mass of the kidney, reduce the kidney function, and eventually lead to kidney failure.
breakdown_text: poly-: many ; cyst: cyst ; -ic: pertaining to

definition: Excessive urination; a common symptom of diabetes. Polyuria is the opposite of oliguria.
A disorder resulting from the compression or obstruction of the urethra due to benign prostatic hyperplasia. Can produce difficulties with urination, including urinary retention.
An inflammation of both the renal pelvis and kidney. Usually caused by a bacterial infection that has spread upward from the bladder.
breakdown_text: pyel/o: renal pelvis ; nephr: kidney ; -itis: inflammation

definition: A surgical incision into the renal pelvis. Performed to remove obstructions such as a stone lodged in the junction between the renal pelvis and the ureter.
breakdown_text: pyel: the renal pelvis ; -otomy: surgical incision

definition: Acute pain in the kidney area that is caused by blockage during the passage of a nephrolith (kidney stone). Colic means spasms of pain in the abdomen. The pain sometimes comes in waves due to the peristaltic movement of the ureters.
The placement of a urinary catheter into the bladder through a small incision made through the abdominal wall just above the pubic bone.
Abbreviated TURP; the removal of excess tissue from an enlarged prostate gland with the use of a resectoscope. Retrograde ejaculation is the most common long-term complication.

Also known as uremic poisoning; a toxic condition resulting from renal failure in which kidney function is compromised and urea and other waste products normally secreted in the urine are retained in the blood.
A stone located anywhere along the ureter.
The discharge of blood from the ureter.
An inflammation of the urethra.
The surgical repair of damage or a defect in the walls of the urethra.
Bleeding from the urethra.
Also known as urethral stricture; narrowing of the urethra. Occurs almost exclusively in men and is caused by scarring from infection or injury.
A surgical incision into the urethra for relief of a stricture. A stricture is an abnormal narrowing of a bodily passage.

Also known as cathing; the insertion of a flexible plastic tube called a catheter into the bladder to withdraw urine for diagnostic purposes, to allow urine to drain freely, or to place a fluid such as a chemotherapy solution.

An abnormal opening between the bladder and vagina that allows constant involuntary flow of urine from the bladder into the vagina. A fistula is an abnormal passage between two internal organs. May be caused by prolonged labor during childbirth or surgery such as a hysterectomy.
breakdown_text: vesic/o: bladder ; vagin: vagina ; -al: pertaining to

definition: A diagnostic procedure in which fluoroscopy is used to examine the flow of urine from the bladder and through the urethra. Often performed after cystography.
breakdown_text: cyst/o: bladder ; urethr/o: urethra ; -graphy: the process of producing a picture or record

definition: Also known as a nephroblastoma; a rare type of malignant tumor of the kidney that occurs in young children. There is a high cure rate when treated promptly.
The process through which the body maintains a constant internal environment.
The major waste product of protein metabolism.
A waste product of muscle metabolism.
Also referred to as the urinary tract; consists of two kidneys, two ureters, one bladder, and one urethra.
The urinary tract and the reproductive organs referred to together because they are located in close proximity.

Two bean-shaped organs that constantly filter the blood to remove waste products and excess water, which are excreted as urine (95% water and 5% urea and other body wastes). Also help maintain proper fluid levels, produce hormones that control blood pressure and make red blood cells, and activate vitamin D to maintain healthy bones.
Pertaining to the kidneys.
breakdown_text: ren: kidney or kidneys ; -al: pertaining to

definition: Behind the peritoneum, which is the membrane that lines the abdominal cavity. The kidneys are located in the retroperitoneal space.
The outer region of the kidney; contains more than one million microscopic units called nephrons. Cortex means the outer portion of an organ.
The inner region of the kidney; contains most of the urine-collecting tubules.
A small tube.
The return to the blood of some of the substances that were removed during filtration.
A cluster of capillaries (plural, glomeruli) within each nephron, surrounded by a cup-shaped membrane called the Bowman's capsule.
A cup-shaped membrane that surrounds the glomerulus.
The part of the nephron into which the remaining filtrate flows; elements including some water, sugar, and electrolytes are returned to the bloodstream via a nearby capillary.
The vessel through which blood enters the kidney and flows into the nephrons.
The vessel through which filtered blood leaves the kidney and returns to the bloodstream.
The funnel-shaped area inside each kidney that is surrounded by the renal cortex and medulla; where the newly formed urine from the nephrons collects before it flows into the ureters.
Two narrow tubes, each about 10 to 12 inches long, which transport urine from the kidney to the bladder. Peristalsis moves urine down each ureter to the bladder.
A series of wave-like contractions that moves urine down each ureter to the bladder; also part of the digestive process.
The openings in the wall of the urinary bladder through which urine drains from the ureters. Orifice means opening.

An oval, hollow, muscular organ that is a reservoir for urine before it is excreted from the body. Located in the anterior portion of the pelvic cavity behind the pubic symphysis; the average adult bladder stores more than one pint of urine.
Folds lining the bladder, as in the stomach, that allow it to expand when full and contract when empty.
The tube extending from the bladder to the exterior of the body.
Two muscular rings, one at either end of the urethra, that control the flow of urine from the bladder into the urethra and out of the urethra through the urethral meatus.
A ring-like muscle that closes a passageway.
Also known as the urinary meatus; the external opening of the urethra. Meatus means the external opening of a canal.
Approximately 1.5 inches long; the urethral meatus is located between the clitoris and the opening of the vagina. Transports only urine.
Approximately 8 inches long; the urethral meatus is located at the tip of the penis. Transports both urine and semen.
A gland of the male reproductive system that surrounds the urethra. Most disorders of the prostate affect the male's ability to urinate.
Also known as voiding or micturition; the normal process of excreting urine. Requires the coordinated contraction of the bladder muscles and relaxation of the sphincters.
A physician who specializes in diagnosing and treating diseases and disorders of the kidneys.
A physician who specializes in diagnosing and treating diseases and disorders of the urinary system of females and the genitourinary system of males.
Kidney disease resulting from poorly controlled diabetes mellitus.

Also known as kidney failure; the inability of one or both of the kidneys to perform their functions. The body cannot replace damaged nephrons, and when too many nephrons have been destroyed, the result is kidney failure.
An elevation of the blood urea nitrogen (BUN) caused by a lack of blood flow to each kidney. Uremia can occur when this excess becomes toxic.
So called because the nephrons look normal under a regular microscope; the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.
An inflammation of the kidney or kidneys. The most common causes are toxins, infection, or an autoimmune disease.
Also known as nephropyosis; suppuration of the kidney, often associated with hydronephrosis. Suppuration means the formation of pus.
breakdown_text: py/o: pus ; nephr: kidney ; -osis: abnormal condition or disease

definition: Spasms of pain in the abdomen.
The most common form of kidney cancer in adults. Can cause flank pain and blood in the urine, but is most commonly asymptomatic until the tumor has grown enough to impair kidney function.

Also known as calculus (plural, calculi); an abnormal mineral deposit that has formed within the body and is named for the organ or tissue where it is located. In the urinary system, stones form when waste products in the urine separate and crystallize.
A blockage that prevents the flow of urine in one part of the urinary tract. Named for their locations, and commonly caused by stones, congenital abnormalities, or an enlarged prostate.
A blockage of one or both ureters. Can be due to congenital abnormality, ureterolith, or other disorders.
Pain in the bladder; also called cystodynia.
Abbreviated VUR; the backward flow of urine into the ureters from the bladder. Most common in infants and children.
breakdown_text: vesic/o: bladder ; ureter: ureter ; -al: pertaining to

definition: An abnormal passage between two internal organs.

The inability to completely empty the bladder when attempting to urinate. More common in men and frequently associated with an enlarged prostate gland. In neurogenic bladder it can result in overflow leakage.
Any disease or damage to a nerve.
One of the most common cancers among men. Can grow slowly with no symptoms, or can grow aggressively and spread throughout the body.

A group of disorders characterized by the inflammation of the prostate gland. The most common type is chronic nonbacterial prostatitis, with no single known cause. Bacterial prostatitis usually results from bacteria transported in the urine.
An abnormal discharge from the urethra. Associated with some sexually transmitted diseases.

Abbreviated UTI; usually begins in the bladder but can affect all parts of the urinary system. Caused by bacteria, most often E. coli, entering the urinary system through the urethra. More frequent in women because the urethra is short and located near the opening to the rectum. In the elderly, often causes weakness and confusion rather than urinary symptoms.
A life-threatening systemic bacterial infection that can occur when a urinary tract infection spreads to the kidneys.
Cystitis that occurs two or more times in six months, or three or more times a year. May require long-term daily antibiotic treatment.
The involuntary discharge of urine.

Difficulty in starting a urinary stream. Most common in older men with enlarged prostate glands. In younger people, the inability to urinate when another person is present is known as bashful bladder syndrome.
The inability to urinate when another person is present, in younger people.
The inability to control the voiding of urine.
Continuous leaking from the bladder either because it is full or because it does not empty completely. Usually caused by a blocked urethra and prevalent in older men with enlarged prostates.
The inability to control the voiding of urine under physical stress such as running, sneezing, laughing, or coughing. Occurs more often in women than in men.

Abbreviated OAB; also known as urge incontinence; occurs when the muscles of the bladder contract involuntarily even though the bladder is not actually full enough to indicate the need to urinate. May result in increased urinary frequency or incontinence.

Abbreviated UA; the examination of urine for the presence of abnormal elements. Used to diagnose diseases, kidney damage, and pregnancy, as well as to detect the presence of substances such as illicit drugs and prescription medications.
breakdown_text: urin: urine ; -alysis: a study of the parts

definition: Abbreviated GFR; a blood test to check how well the kidneys are functioning at filtering blood. Can help diagnose chronic kidney disease and kidney failure.
Abbreviated BUN; a blood test that is an indicator of kidney function.

The use of a handheld ultrasound transducer to look for stones or for elevation of the bladder by an enlarged prostate and to measure the residual amount of urine remaining in the bladder after urination. A normal bladder holds between 300 and 400 mL of urine; when more than this amount is still present after urination, the bladder is described as being distended.
An instrument used for visual examination of internal structures.
A specialized type of endoscope used for visual examination of the urinary bladder; also used for treatment procedures such as the removal of tumors or the reduction of an enlarged prostate gland.
Also known as a CT scan; commonly used to evaluate the urinary system because it can be rapidly performed and provides additional radiographic imaging of the abdomen.
An x-ray or fluoroscopy examination of the bladder after a contrast medium is instilled via a urethral catheter. The resulting film is a cystogram.
breakdown_text: cyst/o: bladder ; -graphy: the process of creating a picture or record

definition: Continuous x-rays projected onto a screen during the examination; can be used to track the flow of contrast or direct an intervention, such as stent placement.
Kidneys, ureters, bladder; an x-ray study without the use of a contrast medium, also referred to as a flat-plate of the abdomen. Used to detect bowel obstructions and nephroliths.

An x-ray of the urinary system taken after a contrast medium has been instilled into one or both ureters through a sterile catheter and caused to flow upward through the urinary tract, usually as part of cystoscopy. Retrograde means moving backward.

Abbreviated DRE; performed on men by using a lubricated, gloved finger placed in the rectum to palpate the prostate gland to detect prostate enlargement and to look for indications of prostate cancer or tumors of the rectum. Digital means using a finger; palpate means the use of touch to examine a body part.

Abbreviated PSA; a protein produced by the cells of the prostate gland to help liquefy semen. The PSA blood test is used to screen for prostate cancer; the higher a man's PSA level, the more likely cancer is present.

Medications administered to increase urine secretion, primarily to rid the body of excess water and salt. Some foods and drinks, such as coffee, tea, and alcoholic beverages, also have a diuretic effect.
Drugs used to block the signals that cause urinary incontinence.
An artificial passage that allows the blood to flow between the body and the hemodialysis unit.
A sterilized solution made up of water and electrolytes contained in the filters of the hemodialysis unit; cleanses the blood by removing waste products and excess fluids.
The minerals that conduct electricity and are found in the body fluid, tissue, and blood.

Abbreviated CAPD; provides ongoing dialysis as the patient goes about daily activities. The dialysate solution is instilled from a plastic container worn under the clothing and about every 4 hours the used solution is drained back into the bag, which is discarded and replaced with a new bag.
Abbreviated CCPD; also known as automated peritoneal dialysis (APD); uses a machine to cycle the dialysate solution during the night while the patient sleeps.
A band of fibers that holds structures together abnormally.

Commonly known as kidney transplant; the grafting of a donor kidney, from either a living or nonliving donor, into the body to replace the recipient's failed kidneys. A single transplanted kidney is capable of adequately performing all kidney functions and frees the patient from the need for dialysis.
The use of shock waves to break up calculi; also used to break up calculi in the ureter, bladder, or urethra.
The surgical removal of a ureter.

A treatment for a nephrolith lodged in the ureter. A specialized instrument called a ureteroscope is inserted through the urethra and bladder into the ureter; if possible, the nephrolith is removed intact, otherwise a laser is used to break it up and the pieces are removed.
The surgical removal of all or part of the urinary bladder. Usually performed to treat bladder cancer.
Also known as urinary ileostomy; the use of a small piece of intestine to convey urine to the ureters and to a stoma in the abdomen.
breakdown_text: ile: ileum or small intestine ; -al: pertaining to

definition: The surgical suturing of a wound or defect in the bladder.

A surgical incision for the removal of a nephrolith from the bladder. No longer common as surgery, but the name is still used to describe a physical examination position for procedures involving the pelvis and lower abdomen.
A flexible plastic tube inserted into the bladder.
A catheter that remains inside the body for a prolonged time based on need; can be either a urethral or a suprapubic catheter. Indwelling means residing within.
Performed by inserting a catheter through the urethra and into the bladder.

The most common type of indwelling catheter; made of a flexible tube with a balloon filled with sterile water at the end to hold it in place in the bladder. Commonly used on postsurgical patients and named for its inventor, surgeon Frederic Foley.
Also known as a short-term catheter; inserted as needed several times a day to drain urine from the bladder.
A surgical incision made in the urethral meatus to enlarge the opening.
The use of high-frequency electrical current to destroy tissue.
The surgical removal of part or all of the prostate gland. Performed to treat prostate cancer or to reduce an enlarged prostate gland; can lead to erectile difficulties.
The surgical removal of the entire prostate gland in cases where it is extremely enlarged or when cancer is suspected.
A specialized endoscopic instrument that resembles a cystoscope, used in a transurethral prostatectomy.
When an orgasm results in semen flowing backward into the bladder instead of out through the penis. The most common long-term complication of a TURP.
An additional treatment used to control prostate cancer.
An additional treatment used to control prostate cancer.
Often the prescribed course of action for prostate cancer in older patients because the disease normally progresses slowly.

A series of pelvic muscle exercises, named for Dr. Arnold Kegel, used to strengthen the muscles of the pelvic floor. Used to control urinary stress incontinence in both sexes, in men to treat prostate pain and swelling, and in women to condition the muscles so that they will recover quickly after childbirth.

Behavioral therapy in which the patient learns to urinate on a schedule, with increasingly longer time intervals as the bladder increases its capacity. The goal is to reestablish voluntary bladder control and to break the cycle of frequency and urgency that results from urge incontinence.
